title: April 2024 Class End of Block Exam

sets.title: Set 1: Original Exam Questions
sets.description: The original MCQs from the April 2024 class Block One Exam paper (PEN 101: Paediatric Nursing I, sat 11 November 2024, Part A, Q1 to Q15).

questions.text: While assessing a 5-month old child, a nurse interprets the milestone as delayed if they find:

options.A: Body weight less than double the birth weight
options.C: Child not able to control the head

questions.explanation: Child not able to control the head (C) is correct because head control is achieved by about 3 to 4 months, so a 5-month-old who cannot hold the head steady has delayed gross motor development and needs further developmental assessment. Body weight less than double the birth weight (A) is not yet abnormal at 5 months, because weight doubles by about 6 months (and quadruples by 2 years). Head circumference of 38 cm (B) is within an acceptable range for a young infant, since head size is judged by plotting it on a growth chart and not by one value. Being unable to sit alone (D) is expected at 5 months, because sitting without support is achieved at about 6 to 8 months.

questions.text: An example of mechanical restraint is:

options.A: Mother holding a child while the nurse is injecting
options.B: Restricting the movement of a child with measles from outside their room
options.C: Administering a sedative to a child with intense itching
options.D: Use of mittens on a child who is itching

questions.explanation: Use of mittens on a child who is itching (D) is correct because a mechanical restraint is a device placed on the body to limit movement of the body or a part of it; mittens cover the whole hand and prevent scratching or pulling out tubes, and other examples are cloth bands, arm boards, elbow restraints, jacket restraints, papoose boards and mummy restraints. A mother holding a child during an injection (A) is a physical restraint (using body contact or bodily force to hold the child). Restricting the movement of a child with measles to their room (B) is an environmental restraint, where the area in which the child can move freely is limited. Giving a sedative to a child with intense itching (C) is a chemical restraint, which uses medicine to calm the child or limit movement. Restraints should be used only when other options have failed, never as punishment, and with consent.

questions.text: In utilizing family centered approach in paediatric nursing practice:

options.A: Children above 7 years are allowed to give consent
options.B: The child's family takes the leadership role in care of the child
options.C: The family is given priority in making decisions for the child
options.D: Medical practice is considered superior to cultural practices

questions.explanation: The family is given priority in making decisions for the child (C) is correct because family-centred care is a partnership with the family, who are the constant in the child's life, and one of its elements is to encourage the family's choices and decision-making, with the parents sharing in decisions about the child's care after receiving complete, unbiased information. Children above 7 years allowed to give consent (A) is incorrect because under the Children Act a child is anyone under 18 years, and consent is given by the parent or guardian (the older child is involved and assent is sought). The family taking the leadership role (B) is incorrect because the partnership is between equals: it does not mean the family leads and the professional follows, nor the reverse. Medical practice superior to cultural practices (D) is incorrect because family-centred care honours racial, ethnic, cultural and socioeconomic diversity, and the nurse is sensitive and flexible.

questions.text: To reduce separation anxiety in a 4-year-old child who is hospitalized, the nurse:

options.A: Allows the child to select the meals they want to eat
options.B: Performs the procedures in the procedure room
options.C: Limits access of the child to frightening experiences
options.D: Allows a familiar person to stay with the child

questions.explanation: Allows a familiar person to stay with the child (D) is correct because separation anxiety (the major reaction of children aged 6 months to 4 years, passing through the phases of protest, despair and detachment) is reduced mainly by encouraging parental participation: a parent or familiar caregiver stays with the child, with a bed or chair provided. Other measures are assigning a familiar primary nurse, keeping the child's routine, allowing safe familiar objects such as toys, and encouraging visits. Allowing the child to select meals (A) helps reduce the feeling of loss of control and autonomy. Performing procedures in the procedure room (B) helps reduce fear by keeping the child's bed a safe place. Limiting access to frightening experiences (C) reduces fear of the unknown and of bodily injury.

questions.text: During triaging, you find the child who has been referred to your hospital and has edema of both feet. The next course of action is:

options.B: Position the child at the front of the queue
options.C: Move the child to the emergency room
options.D: Allow the child to proceed with the usual queue

questions.explanation: Position the child at the front of the queue (B) is correct because oedema of both feet is a priority sign in ETAT (the 'O' in the mnemonic 3 TPR - MOB, indicating kwashiorkor or severe malnutrition), as is a referral note (the 'R' for urgent referral). Children with priority signs are given priority in the queue so that they are assessed and treated without delay, and are weighed and have baseline observations done. Moving the child to the emergency room (C) is for children with emergency signs (obstructed or absent breathing, severe respiratory distress, central cyanosis, signs of shock, coma, convulsions, or severe dehydration with diarrhoea), which this child does not have. Informing the paediatrician on call (A) is not the immediate triage action. Allowing the child to proceed in the usual queue (D) is for non-urgent children with no emergency or priority signs.

questions.text: When triaging a child with breathing problems, the following is evidence of fast breathing in a 9-month old child:
questions.explanation: 52 breaths/min (A) is correct because the cut-off for fast breathing depends on age (breaths are counted for one full minute): 60 or more per minute in a child under 2 months, 50 or more per minute in a child aged 2 to under 12 months, and 40 or more per minute in a child aged 12 months to 5 years. A 9-month-old falls in the 2 to 12 months group, so 50 or more per minute is fast breathing, and 52 meets it. 45 breaths/min (B), 40 breaths/min (C) and 35 breaths/min (D) are all below 50, so they are not fast breathing for this age (40 would be fast only from 12 months).

questions.text: The following childhood disease require airborne isolation precautions:
questions.explanation: Tuberculosis, measles (A) is correct because both are spread by airborne transmission: TB by droplet nuclei generated when a patient coughs, sneezes or sings, and measles by small particles that stay suspended in the air and are spread when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes. Airborne precautions mean a single room with good ventilation (negative pressure if possible) and an N95 respirator for staff. Whooping cough and diphtheria (B) need droplet precautions (contact precautions are added for cutaneous diphtheria). Mumps (C) is spread by droplets and polio is spread by the faecal-oral route, so neither is airborne. Chickenpox (D) is airborne, but neonatal tetanus is not contagious (it is caused by spores from the environment entering the umbilical cord), so the pair is wrong.

questions.text: Treatment of pulmonary tuberculosis in a 10 month old child during intensive phase is:

options.A: 4 months of Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol
options.C: 2 months of Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol

questions.explanation: 2 months of Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol (C) is correct because treatment of TB in children has two phases: the intensive phase lasts 2 months with four drugs (RHZE) given daily, to kill the bacilli rapidly (bactericidal), followed by the continuation phase of 4 months with two drugs (RH) daily to kill the dormant and slowly multiplying bacilli (the continuation phase is extended to 10 months for TB meningitis and bone, joint and spine TB). Paediatric fixed-dose combinations (dispersible RHZ tablets plus E tablets) are used, dosed by weight. 4 months of RHZE (A) is the wrong duration. 4 months of RH (B) describes the continuation phase. 2 months of RH (D) is the wrong drug combination for the intensive phase.

questions.text: To reduce peripheral neuropathy in children receiving tuberculosis treatment:

options.C: Increase the intake of fruits and vegetables

questions.explanation: Initiate pyridoxine supplementation (B) is correct because isoniazid can cause peripheral neuropathy (by interfering with vitamin B6 metabolism), and all children on an isoniazid-containing regimen, whether treatment or preventive therapy, should receive pyridoxine (vitamin B6) throughout the course to prevent or reduce the toxicity. Administering the drugs before meals (A) is not related to neuropathy; anti-TB drugs are usually given together once a day on an empty stomach for better absorption. Increasing the intake of fruits and vegetables (C) is good nutrition but does not prevent isoniazid neuropathy. Giving the smallest dose possible (D) is wrong, because under-dosing leads to treatment failure and drug resistance; doses are given according to body weight.

questions.text: A correct statement regarding neonatal tetanus is:

options.A: One attack confers the child with lifelong immunity
options.B: Is prevented by vaccinating the child with tetanus toxoid
options.C: The source of infection is a case of neonatal tetanus
options.D: The child presents with inability to breastfeed

questions.explanation: The child presents with inability to breastfeed (D) is correct because the toxin causes trismus (lockjaw) from rigidity of the masseter muscles, so the baby cannot open the mouth or suck. The case definition is a newborn who sucked and cried normally in the first 2 days of life, but between 3 and 28 days cannot suck normally and has generalised stiffness or spasms. One attack confers lifelong immunity (A) is false: clinical tetanus does not produce immunity, and survivors need active immunisation with tetanus toxoid. Prevented by vaccinating the child (B) is false: neonatal tetanus is prevented by immunising pregnant women with tetanus toxoid (so that protective antibodies cross to the baby), together with clean delivery and cord care (clean hands, clean blade, clean dressing). The source of infection being a case of neonatal tetanus (C) is false because tetanus is not passed from person to person; the source is Clostridium tetani spores in soil, dust and animal and human faeces that enter through the umbilical cord.

options.A: The spores gain access to the body through the respiratory system
options.B: The bacteria toxin causes inflammation and formation of a pseudo membrane
options.C: The toxin interferes with neuromuscular transmission of impulses
options.D: The bacteria attach to the cilia of the respiratory epithelial cells

questions.explanation: The bacteria toxin causes inflammation and formation of a pseudo membrane (B) is correct because Corynebacterium diphtheriae settles on the mucosa of the upper respiratory tract, multiplies and releases an exotoxin, which causes a local inflammatory reaction in which the exudate forms a grey to black, adherent pseudo-membrane that can obstruct the airway; the toxin is also carried in the blood and damages the heart (myocarditis), nerves and kidneys. The spores gaining access through the respiratory system (A) is not correct because C. diphtheriae is a non-spore-forming bacillus, and spores are a feature of Clostridium tetani (which enters through the umbilical cord or wounds). The toxin interfering with neuromuscular transmission (C) describes tetanus (tetanospasmin). The bacteria attaching to the cilia of the respiratory epithelial cells (D) describes whooping cough (Bordetella pertussis), whose toxins paralyse the cilia.

Erythromycin, gentle suctioning (A) is correct because the management of whooping cough includes erythromycin 30 to 50 mg/kg QID for 10 days (azithromycin or clarithromycin are alternatives), droplet isolation, oxygen therapy, gentle suctioning of secretions, a calm quiet environment, feeding and fluid therapy, and admission for severe illness or a child under 3 months. Vaccination with DPT (B) is prevention (DPT in the pentavalent vaccine at 6, 10 and 14 weeks) and is not part of treating an infected child, although increased fluids are part of care. Diazepam and antitoxin (C) are used in tetanus (diazepam to control spasms) and diphtheria (antitoxin to neutralise the toxin). Crystalline penicillin with oxygen therapy (D) is not the treatment of choice, since penicillin is used for diphtheria (and pertussis responds to macrolides), although oxygen therapy is appropriate.

questions.text: A correct statement regarding Mumps infection is:

options.A: The hall mark is bilateral swelling of the parotid glands
options.B: The multiplication of the virus occurs in the nasopharynx
options.C: Can be prevented by immunizing all children at birth
options.D: One infection does not confer lifelong immunity

questions.explanation: The multiplication of the virus occurs in the nasopharynx (B) is correct because in the pathogenesis of mumps the virus is transmitted by the respiratory route (droplets), replicates in the nasopharynx and regional lymph nodes, then spreads through the blood (viraemia) to the salivary glands, meninges, pancreas, testes and ovaries. The hallmark being bilateral swelling of the parotid glands (A) is not exact: the hallmark is swelling of one or more salivary glands, typically the parotids, and it may be unilateral or bilateral. Immunising all children at birth (C) is incorrect because the MMR vaccine is not given at birth (it is given in later infancy), and it is not part of the free routine KEPI schedule in Kenya but is available in private hospitals. One infection not conferring lifelong immunity (D) is incorrect because mumps infection gives lifelong immunity.

questions.text: The vitamin A dose for Baby G, 4 months old who has measles is:
questions.explanation: 50,000 IU (A) is correct because vitamin A supplementation reduces the mortality and morbidity of measles and is given to all children with measles, especially those who are malnourished, with the dose based on age: 50,000 IU for 0 to 6 months (and for babies under 6 months), 100,000 IU for 6 to 12 months, and 200,000 IU for above 1 year. Baby G is 4 months old, so the dose is 50,000 IU. Two doses are given, 24 hours apart (a third dose 2 to 4 weeks later if eye signs are present or the child is severely malnourished). 75,000 IU (B) is not a standard dose. 100,000 IU (C) is the dose for 6 to 12 months. 200,000 IU (D) is the dose for children above 1 year.

questions.text: A true statement regarding poliomyelitis is:

options.B: The patient reports loss of sensation in the affected limbs
options.C: The incidence between the lower and upper limbs is equal
options.D: In the post paralytic stage, shortening of the limb can occur

questions.explanation: In the post paralytic stage, shortening of the limb can occur (D) is correct because in the post-paralytic stage the residual disability includes deformities and contractures, coldness and cyanosis of the affected limb, and retarded bone growth leading to shortening of the limb, with slow recovery for up to 2 years. The paralysis being symmetrical (A) is false: it is asymmetrical and flaccid, descending, and the muscles are painful and floppy with diminished reflexes. Loss of sensation (B) is false because sensation remains intact (the virus destroys only the motor neurons of the anterior horn cells). Equal incidence in the lower and upper limbs (C) is false because the lower limbs are more commonly affected than the upper limbs.
